question.title: Pair indices for a target

question.title: Same letters, different order
question.summary: Decide whether two lowercase English strings contain exactly the same letters with the same multiplicities. Letter order does not matter. Empty strings are permitted.

examples.explanation: Each letter occurs once in both strings.

approaches.title: Letter frequency balance
approaches.explanation: Reject unequal lengths, then count each letter from the first string and subtract letters from the second. Every final count must be zero.
approaches.pseudocode:
if lengths differ: return false
counts = 26 zeros
for letter in first: counts[letter] += 1
for letter in second: counts[letter] -= 1
return every count is zero
approaches.assumptions: The alphabet has exactly 26 letters.

question.title: Products without the current position
question.summary: For each position, compute the product of every other array value. Do not use division. Zeros and negative values are valid. Return a new array; the input must remain unchanged.

content.description: For each position, compute the product of every other array value. Do not use division. Zeros and negative values are valid. Return a new array; the input must remain unchanged.
content.input_format: values: integer array.
content.output_format: An array of products with the same length.
constraints: All intermediate products fit in a signed 64-bit integer

examples.explanation: Each result excludes the value at its own position.
Only the zero position excludes the zero from its product.

hints: Each answer is a product to the left multiplied by a product to the right.
Store left products in the output, then walk backwards.

content.verification: Published examples checked with the included reference implementation. Complexity analysis describes the stated approach.

approaches.title: Prefix and suffix products
approaches.explanation: Write the product strictly to the left at each position. A backwards pass multiplies in the product strictly to the right.
approaches.pseudocode:
out = array of ones
prefix = 1
for i from left to right:
  out[i] = prefix; prefix *= values[i]
suffix = 1
for i from right to left:
  out[i] *= suffix; suffix *= values[i]
return out
approaches.assumptions: Input and result storage are excluded from auxiliary space.

question.title: Best contiguous total
tags: Solve Problems on Arrays [Easy -> Medium -> Hard]
question.summary: Find the largest possible sum of a nonempty contiguous segment of an integer array. Return the sum, not the segment. An all-negative array must still select one element.

content.description: Find the largest possible sum of a nonempty contiguous segment of an integer array. Return the sum, not the segment. An all-negative array must still select one element.
content.input_format: values: nonempty integer array.

examples.explanation: The segment [6,-2,5] totals 9.
The best nonempty segment is [-3].

hints: At each position, either extend the previous segment or start again.
Keep the best total seen anywhere separately.

approaches.title: Kadane recurrence
approaches.explanation: The best segment ending here is either the current value alone or that value added to the previous ending total. Take the maximum over all positions.
approaches.pseudocode:
ending = best = values[0]
for x after the first value:
  ending = max(x, ending + x)
  best = max(best, ending)
return best
approaches.assumptions: Sums fit in the chosen integer type.

approaches.title: Enumerate starting positions
approaches.explanation: For each start, extend a running sum through every possible end. Never choose an empty segment.
approaches.assumptions: A running sum avoids a third scan for each segment.

question.title: Merge touching ranges
tags: Solve Problems on Arrays [Easy -> Medium -> Hard]
question.summary: Merge a list of closed numeric intervals. Intervals overlap when they share any point, including an endpoint. Return disjoint merged intervals ordered by their starting points.

content.description: Merge a list of closed numeric intervals. Intervals overlap when they share any point, including an endpoint. Return disjoint merged intervals ordered by their starting points.
content.input_format: intervals: array of [start,end] pairs.

examples.explanation: The shared endpoints connect all three intervals.
There are no ranges to merge.

hints: Order intervals by their start.

content.verification: Published examples checked with the included reference implementation. Complexity analysis describes the stated approach.

approaches.title: Sort then sweep
approaches.explanation: After sorting by start, extend the last result when the next start is at most its end. Otherwise begin a new range.
approaches.pseudocode:
sort intervals by start
result = []
for [start,end] in sorted intervals:
  if result is nonempty and start <= result.last.end:
    result.last.end = max(result.last.end, end)
  else: append [start,end]
return result
approaches.space_complexity: O(n) including a sorted copy and result
approaches.assumptions: Sorting space depends on the implementation; this bound permits a copy.

question.title: Locate a value in sorted data
question.summary: Locate a target in an ascending array of distinct integers. Return its zero-based index, or -1 if absent. Use logarithmic search rather than checking every element.

content.description: Locate a target in an ascending array of distinct integers. Return its zero-based index, or -1 if absent. Use logarithmic search rather than checking every element.
content.input_format: values: sorted distinct integers; target: integer.

examples.explanation: Index 2 contains the target.
The empty array has no matching position.

hints: Compare the target with the midpoint.
Keep both ends of the remaining candidate range.
content.authorship: Independently authored for DSA Space. Related platform links are practice references, not the source of this stored text.
content.verification: Published examples checked with the included reference implementation. Complexity analysis describes the stated approach.

approaches.title: Closed-interval binary search
approaches.explanation: A midpoint comparison removes the half that cannot contain the target. Continue while the inclusive search interval is nonempty.
approaches.pseudocode:
left = 0; right = n - 1
while left <= right:
  mid = left + floor((right-left)/2)
  if values[mid] == target: return mid
  if values[mid] < target: left = mid + 1
  else: right = mid - 1
return -1
approaches.assumptions: Random-access array; values are distinct and sorted.

approaches.title: Two boundary searches
approaches.explanation: Use binary search for the lower bound and upper bound. If the lower bound does not equal the target, return the missing result.
approaches.pseudocode:
first = lower_bound(values, target)
if first == n or values[first] != target: return [-1,-1]
after = upper_bound(values, target)
return [first, after - 1]
approaches.assumptions: Use direct comparisons for upper_bound to avoid target+1 overflow.

question.title: Floor of a square root
question.summary: For a nonnegative integer, return the largest integer whose square is no greater than that value. Do not call a square-root function.

content.description: For a nonnegative integer, return the largest integer whose square is no greater than that value. Do not call a square-root function.
content.input_format: value: nonnegative integer.
content.output_format: The integer floor of its square root.

examples.explanation: 25 ≤ 26, while 36 is too large.
The square root of zero is zero.

hints: The predicate candidate² ≤ value is monotonic.
Remember the largest candidate that satisfies it.
content.authorship: Independently authored for DSA Space. Related platform links are practice references, not the source of this stored text.
content.verification: Published examples checked with the included reference implementation. Complexity analysis describes the stated approach.

approaches.title: Binary search on the answer
approaches.explanation: Search integer candidates. A valid candidate allows searching higher; an invalid candidate forces the upper boundary lower.
approaches.pseudocode:
left = 0; right = value
while left <= right:
  mid = left + floor((right-left)/2)
  if mid == 0 or mid <= value / mid: left = mid + 1
  else: right = mid - 1
return right
approaches.assumptions: Division comparison avoids overflow in fixed-width integer languages.

question.summary: Check whether a string reads the same forwards and backwards after ignoring ASCII punctuation and spaces and treating letters case-insensitively. Keep digits. A string with no letters or digits is a palindrome.

approaches.title: Inward pointers
approaches.explanation: Advance each pointer past non-alphanumeric characters, compare lowercase characters, then move both inward.
approaches.pseudocode:
left = 0; right = length - 1
while left < right:
  skip ignored characters on both sides
  if retained characters differ ignoring case: return false
  left += 1; right -= 1
return true
approaches.assumptions: ASCII character checks take constant time.

question.title: Pair in sorted data
question.summary: Find two distinct elements in a nondecreasing integer array that sum to a target. Return their one-based positions in increasing order. The input has at most one valid pair; return [] if absent.

content.description: Find two distinct elements in a nondecreasing integer array that sum to a target. Return their one-based positions in increasing order. The input has at most one valid pair; return [] if absent.

examples.explanation: The values 4 and 6 sum to 10.

content.authorship: Independently authored for DSA Space. Related platform links are practice references, not the source of this stored text.

approaches.title: Opposite-end pointers
approaches.explanation: If the sum is too small, discard the left endpoint; if too large, discard the right endpoint. Sorted order justifies each discarded candidate.
approaches.pseudocode:
left = 0; right = n - 1
while left < right:
  sum = values[left] + values[right]
  if sum == target: return [left+1,right+1]
  if sum < target: left += 1
  else: right -= 1
return []
approaches.assumptions: The input is already sorted.

question.title: Water between two walls
question.summary: At each integer position there is a vertical wall with a given nonnegative height. Choose two walls to maximize the area between them: distance multiplied by the shorter height. Return zero if fewer than two walls exist.

content.description: At each integer position there is a vertical wall with a given nonnegative height. Choose two walls to maximize the area between them: distance multiplied by the shorter height. Return zero if fewer than two walls exist.
content.input_format: heights: array of nonnegative integers.

examples.explanation: Positions 0 and 4 enclose width 4 and height 3.
One wall cannot enclose water.

hints: The shorter wall limits the area.
Keeping that shorter wall while reducing width cannot improve the area.
content.authorship: Independently authored for DSA Space. Related platform links are practice references, not the source of this stored text.
content.verification: Published examples checked with the included reference implementation. Complexity analysis describes the stated approach.

approaches.title: Move the limiting wall
approaches.explanation: Evaluate the outermost pair and move a pointer at the shorter wall inward. A better area must replace a limiting height.
approaches.pseudocode:
left = 0; right = n - 1; best = 0
while left < right:
  best = max(best, (right-left) * min(heights[left],heights[right]))
  move the pointer at the shorter wall inward
return best
approaches.assumptions: Use an integer type large enough for height times width.

approaches.title: Stable compaction
approaches.explanation: Scan once to write nonzero values from the front. Fill the unwritten suffix with zeros.
approaches.pseudocode:
write = 0
for x in values:
  if x != 0: values[write] = x; write += 1
while write < n: values[write] = 0; write += 1
return values
approaches.assumptions: The JSON reference harness copies input only to isolate test cases.

question.title: Shortest positive-sum window
question.summary: Find the minimum length of a nonempty contiguous subarray whose sum is at least a positive target. All array values are positive. Return zero when no qualifying window exists.

content.description: Find the minimum length of a nonempty contiguous subarray whose sum is at least a positive target. All array values are positive. Return zero when no qualifying window exists.
content.input_format: values: positive integer array; target: positive integer.

examples.explanation: The final pair [3,5] reaches 8.
Even the whole array is too small.

hints: Positive values make the window sum monotonic as an edge moves.
Shrink the left edge whenever the target is reached.
content.authorship: Independently authored for DSA Space. Related platform links are practice references, not the source of this stored text.
content.verification: Published examples checked with the included reference implementation. Complexity analysis describes the stated approach.

approaches.title: Expand and shrink
approaches.explanation: Add values at the right edge. While the sum qualifies, record the length and remove the leftmost value to seek a shorter window.
approaches.pseudocode:
left = 0; sum = 0; best = infinity
for right from 0 to n-1:
  sum += values[right]
  while sum >= target:
    best = min(best, right-left+1)
    sum -= values[left]; left += 1
return 0 if best is infinity else best
approaches.assumptions: Strictly positive inputs are essential; this method is not valid for arbitrary negative values.

question.title: Maximum in every fixed window
tags: Stack and Queues [Learning, Pre-In-Post-fix, Monotonic Stack, Implementation]
question.summary: For every contiguous window of exactly k elements, report its maximum. Slide the window one position at a time from left to right.

content.description: For every contiguous window of exactly k elements, report its maximum. Slide the window one position at a time from left to right.
content.input_format: values: integer array; k: window length.

examples.explanation: The three windows have maxima 4,5,5.
Each one-element window reports its own value.

hints: An older smaller value becomes useless when a newer larger value arrives.
Keep candidate indices in decreasing value order.
content.authorship: Independently authored for DSA Space. Related platform links are practice references, not the source of this stored text.
content.verification: Published examples checked with the included reference implementation. Complexity analysis describes the stated approach.

approaches.title: Monotonic deque
approaches.explanation: Remove expired indices from the front and dominated indices from the back. The front always identifies the current maximum.
approaches.pseudocode:
deque = empty double-ended queue
for i from 0 to n-1:
  remove front indices <= i-k
  remove back indices whose values <= values[i]
  append i
  if i >= k-1: append values[deque.front] to result
return result
approaches.assumptions: Each index enters and leaves the deque at most once; use a bounded deque.

approaches.title: Scan each window
approaches.explanation: Compute every window maximum by examining its k elements.
approaches.pseudocode:
for start from 0 to n-k:
  append max(values[start:start+k])
approaches.assumptions: Scan by index rather than allocating window slices.

approaches.title: Iterative pointer reversal
approaches.explanation: Redirect the current node toward the already reversed prefix, then advance using the saved original next pointer.

previous = null; current = head
while current != null:
  next = current.next
  current.next = previous
  previous = current; current = next
return previous
approaches.assumptions: Serialization and test-harness list construction are excluded.

examples.explanation: Use blue, bird, then blue again.
The trailing s cannot be covered.

approaches.title: Prefix reachability
approaches.explanation: For each ending position, try each dictionary word. A matching suffix whose preceding prefix is reachable makes the current prefix reachable.
approaches.assumptions: w is dictionary size and L maximum word length; substring comparison is not treated as constant time.

question.title: Reach the final position
question.summary: From position zero, a nonnegative array value gives the maximum forward jump length available there. Decide whether the final position is reachable. A one-element array is already finished.

content.description: From position zero, a nonnegative array value gives the maximum forward jump length available there. Decide whether the final position is reachable. A one-element array is already finished.
content.input_format: jumps: nonempty array of nonnegative integers.

examples.explanation: Jump from 0 to 2 and then to 4.
Position 1 cannot move and position 2 is unreachable.

hints: Track the furthest index reachable from positions already processed.
An index beyond that frontier cannot be visited.
content.authorship: Independently authored for DSA Space. Related platform links are practice references, not the source of this stored text.
content.verification: Published examples checked with the included reference implementation. Complexity analysis describes the stated approach.

approaches.title: Reachability frontier
approaches.explanation: Scan positions in order. If an index exceeds the reachable frontier, fail; otherwise extend the frontier using its jump length.
approaches.pseudocode:
furthest = 0
for i from 0 to n-1:
  if i > furthest: return false
  furthest = max(furthest, i+jumps[i])
return true
approaches.assumptions: Jumps are forward and nonnegative.

question.title: Remove overlapping appointments
question.summary: Find the minimum number of intervals to remove so the remainder do not overlap. Intervals are half-open [start,end), so an appointment ending when another starts is compatible.

content.description: Find the minimum number of intervals to remove so the remainder do not overlap. Intervals are half-open [start,end), so an appointment ending when another starts is compatible.
content.input_format: intervals: array of [start,end] pairs.

examples.explanation: Keep [1,3) and [3,5), removing [2,4).
Touching endpoints are compatible here.

hints: Minimizing removals is the same as maximizing kept intervals.
Choosing the earliest finish leaves the most room for later appointments.
content.authorship: Independently authored for DSA Space. Related platform links are practice references, not the source of this stored text.

approaches.title: Earliest-finish selection
approaches.explanation: Sort intervals by end. Keep a range whenever its start is at least the end of the last kept range.
approaches.pseudocode:
sort by end ascending
lastEnd = -infinity; kept = 0
for [start,end] in intervals:
  if start >= lastEnd: kept += 1; lastEnd = end
return intervalCount - kept
approaches.assumptions: Sorting storage depends on implementation; this version preserves the input.

question.summary: Count the number of 1 bits in the unsigned 32-bit binary representation of a nonnegative integer.

examples.explanation: 13 is binary 1101.
Zero has no set bits.

hints: Subtracting one changes the lowest set bit and the zeros below it.
n AND (n-1) clears exactly one set bit.

approaches.title: Clear the lowest set bit
approaches.explanation: Repeatedly remove one set bit until the value becomes zero, counting iterations.
approaches.pseudocode:
count = 0
while value != 0:
  value = value AND (value - 1)
  count += 1
return count
approaches.assumptions: b is the number of set bits. JavaScript must normalize bitwise results to unsigned 32-bit.

question.title: Answer immutable range sums
question.summary: Preprocess an integer array to answer many inclusive range-sum queries. The array does not change between queries. Indices are zero-based.

content.description: Preprocess an integer array to answer many inclusive range-sum queries. The array does not change between queries. Indices are zero-based.
content.input_format: values: integer array; queries: [left,right] pairs.
content.output_format: The sum for each query in order.
constraints: Every query satisfies 0 ≤ left ≤ right < n
An empty array has no queries

examples.explanation: The queried sums are 4-1+3 and -1+3+2.
There are no ranges to answer.

hints: Keep sums of prefixes ending before each position.
Subtract the prefix before left from the prefix after right.
content.authorship: Independently authored for DSA Space. Related platform links are practice references, not the source of this stored text.
content.verification: Published examples checked with the included reference implementation. Complexity analysis describes the stated approach.

approaches.title: Prefix-sum array
approaches.explanation: Build a prefix array of length n+1 beginning with zero. Each inclusive range sum is prefix[right+1]-prefix[left].
approaches.pseudocode:
prefix[0] = 0
for i from 0 to n-1: prefix[i+1] = prefix[i]+values[i]
for [left,right] in queries: output prefix[right+1]-prefix[left]
approaches.time_complexity: O(n + q) total; O(1) per query
approaches.assumptions: q is query count; accumulated sums must fit the numeric type.

approaches.title: Sum every requested range
approaches.explanation: Answer each query by scanning its inclusive range.
approaches.pseudocode:
for [left,right] in queries:
  sum = 0
  for i from left to right: sum += values[i]
  output sum
approaches.assumptions: Reasonable only when queries are few or ranges short.

question.title: Queue built from two stacks
tags: Stack and Queues [Learning, Pre-In-Post-fix, Monotonic Stack, Implementation]
question.summary: Implement FIFO queue operations push, pop, peek and empty using only two LIFO stacks. Return answers for pop, peek and empty; push has no output. Pop and peek occur only when the queue is nonempty.

content.description: Implement FIFO queue operations push, pop, peek and empty using only two LIFO stacks. Return answers for pop, peek and empty; push has no output. Pop and peek occur only when the queue is nonempty.
content.input_format: operations: arrays such as ["push",4], ["pop"], ["peek"], ["empty"].

examples.explanation: The earliest pushed value leaves first.
A newly created queue is empty.

hints: Reversing a stack exposes the oldest item.
Transfer only when the output stack is empty.
content.authorship: Independently authored for DSA Space. Related platform links are practice references, not the source of this stored text.
content.verification: Published examples checked with the included reference implementation. Complexity analysis describes the stated approach.

approaches.title: Lazy stack transfer
approaches.explanation: Push into an input stack. For pop or peek, move all input items to an empty output stack, then use its top.
approaches.pseudocode:
push(x): input.push(x)
ensureOutput():
  if output empty: while input nonempty: output.push(input.pop())
pop(): ensureOutput(); return output.pop()
peek(): ensureOutput(); return output.top
empty(): return both stacks empty
approaches.time_complexity: O(1) amortized; O(n) worst case for one transfer
approaches.assumptions: Each value transfers between stacks at most once before removal.

question.title: Range sums with point assignments
question.summary: Maintain an integer array while processing point assignments and inclusive range-sum queries. A set operation replaces a value; it does not add to it. All indices in this independently authored exercise are zero-based.

content.description: Maintain an integer array while processing point assignments and inclusive range-sum queries. A set operation replaces a value; it does not add to it. All indices in this independently authored exercise are zero-based.
content.input_format: values: nonempty array; operations: ["set",index,value] or ["sum",left,right].
constraints: All indices and ranges are valid

examples.explanation: The assignment changes index 2 from 1 to 7.
Assignments may reduce a value or make it negative.

hints: A normal prefix array is expensive to update.
A Fenwick tree stores reusable partial sums; assignments become difference updates.
content.authorship: Independently authored for DSA Space. Related platform links are practice references, not the source of this stored text.
content.verification: Published examples checked with the included reference implementation. Complexity analysis describes the stated approach.

approaches.title: Fenwick tree plus current values
approaches.explanation: Build a one-based Fenwick tree. To assign, add new-old along the index’s update path. A range sum subtracts two prefix sums.
approaches.pseudocode:
build current values and Fenwick tree
set(index,value):
  delta = value-current[index]; current[index] = value
  add delta at Fenwick index index+1 and successive i += lowbit(i)
sum(left,right): return prefix(right+1)-prefix(left)
prefix(count): accumulate tree[i] while i -= lowbit(i)
approaches.time_complexity: O(n log n) build; O(log n) per operation
approaches.assumptions: This build inserts each value separately; an O(n) build is also possible. Sums use sufficiently wide integers.
